newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Italy govt united on welfare reform - Prodi.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italy govt united on welfare reform - Prodi.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi, walking a political tightrope over the cuts to Italy's costly pensions bill, said on Tuesday his centre-left coalition government was united on the need to tackle reforms to the welfare state.

"There are absolutely no differences within the government on the issue of how to confront reform of the welfare state, which must in any case remain a means of defending the weakest," Prodi told a news conference.

Prodi is caught between a need to reduce the public deficit in order to stay in sight of European single currency goals, and opposition to social spending cuts from a key parliamentary ally, the Communist Refoundation party.

The hard-left group, which Prodi depends upon for a majority in parliament, got its way over welfare spending in the 1997 austerity budget and has vowed to bring down the government if it cuts social spending.

Opposition centre-right leader Silvio Berlusconi turned up the temperature in an increasingly heated debate, offering to work with the coalition on an early 1998 budget in return for a combined assault on welfare reform.

Berlusconi wrote in a letter to the Rome newspaper Il Messaggero that it was time to reform "abnormal pensions spending which makes Italy's entry into and ability to remain in a single currency Europe less than credible".
"We are and remain ready to review pensions spending as soon as possible without devastating the welfare state," he wrote.

But he urged Massimo D'Alema, whose ex-communist Democratic Party of the Left is the biggest in Prodi's coalition, to tell Communist Refoundation and trades union "sirens" in no uncertain terms that welfare costs had to be cut.
According to European Union statistics, Italy spends less overall on its social services than the European average, but more on pensions.

Italy pushed through some pension reforms in 1995 and agreed to review the situation in 1998, but a row has broken out over moves to bring the review forward to this year. Communist Refoundation and union leaders have signalled fierce opposition.

Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said in an interview published on Monday that some adjustment to Italy's social spending was "probable" and as far as he was concerned, the sooner it happened the better.
Prodi told the news conference there was no question of altering pensions until an in-depth review had been carried out.

He said a commission studying social service spending would complete its work within a few weeks and his coalition was in continuous dialogue with Communist Refoundation. He added that he was certain "points of convergence" would emerge.

Berlusconi, in his article, linked the issue of welfare reform with a government proposal to bring forward the 1998 budget to show Italy's will to stop at nothing to be in shape for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) at its planned start in 1999.
Opposition support for the budget proposal could be vital but Berlusconi has said his support would depend on guarantees on its contents, something Prodi has rejected.
Berlusconi, in a radio interview earlier, denied he had a hidden motive in offering co-operation with the government, and said it was not his intention to "unhinge" Prodi's coalition.
